written.myAnswer: Strong intermolecular forces keep the molecules of a solid close together at fixed positions. They can only vibrate about those positions, so the solid has a definite shape and volume.
Gas molecules are far apart and move freely in all directions, spreading to fill their container. Therefore, a gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.
In a solid, molecules are very close together; in a liquid, they are close together but can move past one another; in a gas, they are far apart.
Raising a liquid’s temperature increases the average kinetic energy of its molecules, so they move more vigorously.
Yes. The kinetic molecular theory applies in the sense that plasma particles are in constant motion. Plasma contains freely moving positive ions and electrons, making it a conducting state of matter.
Gas molecules continually collide and exchange energy, so their kinetic energies and speeds differ; they do not all move at the same speed at a given instant.

In solids, strong intermolecular forces hold molecules at fixed positions, where they vibrate; solids therefore have definite shape and volume. In liquids, molecules remain close together but can slide past one another, so liquids have definite volume but no definite shape. In gases, molecules are far apart and move freely, so gases have neither definite shape nor definite volume.
